content.text:
**Your #1238 fixes are verified and ruled clean — no seventh review round needed ([ruling 4893689718](https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1238#issuecomment-4893689718)).** The fence fix is exactly the right shape (the two-leg proof keeps its full strength — I checked it still catches the original bug), the fixture regen is the intentional value, and the BVS change is twelve mechanical lines a trait change forced, in a non-live crate. The round-6 approvals still cover the real settlement code.

**Right now:** a queue attempt is running (started 13:55Z) — verdict lands around 14:45Z. Nothing to do until then.

**If it fails again, stop batching — that's my main recommendation.** Here's the plain-English problem: Mergify has been testing all three PRs *together* in one batch. One bad PR fails the whole batch, everyone gets thrown out, and the failure isn't always attributable. Three PRs × repeated batches is how you get the churn you're seeing. The robust path:

1. **Dequeue everything**, then queue **#1238 alone** (`@mergifyio queue` on just it). It's the most thoroughly verified of the three — six review rounds plus today's verified fixes — and its two known full-suite failures are fixed. Once it merges, it's locked in.
2. Then **#1258 alone**, then **#1255 alone**. Both touch CI machinery itself, which is exactly the kind of change that can poison a shared batch — they should each prove themselves solo. (Their content is your/Codex's series per our division of labor; I'm only sequencing.)

Serial queueing costs maybe an hour more in total, but every success is final and every failure points at exactly one PR — no more collective punishment.

**One caution:** #1255's head has moved since its last review state I have on record. If its own review isn't complete, merge order matters even more — #1238 and #1258 shouldn't wait behind it. Ping me when the current attempt resolves either way, and if #1238 merges I'll immediately run the post-merge checks (#1179 open, fifteenth campaign PR recorded) and set up the campaign's wrap-up phase.
so what's the reason behind this?

Three reasons stack, and none of them is randomness:

**1. The queue is now the first place the full test suite ever runs.** That's a direct consequence of the CI protocol we adopted (correctly) to stop the 52-minute proof runs. Workers iterate on small targeted test filters; the full ~3,200-test suite runs only at the queue. So any failure living *outside* a PR's targeted filter — and every failure this week was that kind — gets discovered inside the queue instead of before it. We traded expensive early proof for cheap iteration plus queue-time discovery. This week is the first time we're paying the discovery side of that trade.

**2. Batching turns one failure into three dequeues.** Mergify tests the three PRs *together*. Each PR carried one latent failure of its own; each batch attempt died on whichever surfaced first, threw all three out, and the next attempt died on a *different* PR's issue. That's why it feels like endless churn — it's actually three separate one-time failures being discovered serially while collectively punished. That's why I recommend queueing one PR at a time.

**3. The failures themselves are all one species: repo-wide guard tests tripped by cross-cutting changes.** The repo deliberately has global tripwires — a frozen config snapshot, import fences, CI-registry consistency checks, mandatory trait methods. Each of these three PRs changed something global (a config key, a trait's required methods, a CI registry field), and the guard for a global thing never lives in the feature's own test filter. So: guard trips at the queue, nowhere earlier. Note these are the fences doing their job — every single trip was a real inconsistency, fixed within hours.

**The lasting fix**, beyond serializing this batch: add a standard "pre-queue guard" test filter to the protocol — the known global tripwires (frozen fixtures, fence tests, config parsing, workspace compile) run as one last debug-lane pass before anyone queues. That's minutes, not 52, and it would have caught all of this week's failures before the queue. I'll fold that into the worker instructions once these three are merged.

content.text:
Yes — and you've caught me proposing a second mechanism where one already exists. I went and checked what the preflight actually runs before answering, and the finding explains everything:

**The preflight exists for exactly this role, but its guard set is one narrow slice.** `merge_queue_preflight.py` runs the *static fence battery* (the ~107-second script suite — 44 static fences plus their infrastructure tests) against each PR and the batch. That's all. It does not compile the Rust workspace, does not run any Rust tests, and does not run the CI-governance derivation check.

Now map this week's four queue failures against that:
- BVS missing trait methods → a **compile** failure. Preflight doesn't compile. Miss.
- Frozen config snapshot → a **Rust test**. Preflight runs no Rust tests. Miss.
- The import fence that #1238 tripped → the bitter one: this repo enforces fences on *two* surfaces — the static battery (which passed everywhere, locally and in preflight) and a separate *Rust-test* variant of the same fence, which is the one that fired. Preflight only runs the first surface. Miss.
- #1258's registry drift → surfaced by the coverage-enforcer, which preflight doesn't run. Miss.

So the preflight didn't fail at its job — it was scoped, by design, as "fast advisory + batch-split advice, the queue CI is the real gate." **What broke the balance is our own CI protocol change:** when we stopped running full CI before queueing, the queue became the first full-suite run, which silently widened the gap between what preflight guards and what the queue fails on. Nobody re-scoped the preflight when we made that trade.

**So the correct fix is what you implied:** extend the *preflight's* guard set — one owned definition — rather than invent a parallel "pre-queue filter." Concretely: a guard profile of workspace compile-check + the known Rust tripwire tests (frozen fixtures, fence-test variants, config parsing) + the registry derivation check, defined once and consumed by the preflight (or the last debug-lane run — same profile either way). Conveniently, there's already an open issue redesigning preflight profiles (#1252, the latency work), so this lands as an addendum to that scope, not a new mechanism — and #1255, sitting in your stuck batch, is part of that same redesign.

Immediate plan stands: serialize the queue (#1238 first), and once the three are merged I'll write the preflight-scope addendum into #1252.
